metadata.document: Submission on Proposed Amendments to the Biosecurity Act 1993

cleaned_body_text: Submission on Proposed Amendments to the Biosecurity Act 1993. SUBMITTER DETAILS: FULL NAME: Environmental Defence Society Incorporated, ADDRESS: PO Box 91736, Victoria Street West, Auckland 1142, CONTACT: Fernanda Caballero / Deidre Koolen-Bourke, EMAIL: fernanda@eds.org.nz / deidre@eds.org.nz. Introduction: 1. This is a submission by the Environmental Defence Society (EDS) on proposed amendments to the Biosecurity Act 1993 (Act) as set out in the Ministry for Primary Industries’ Discussion Documents. 2. EDS is an apolitical, not-for-profit organisation dedicated to achieving improved outcomes for New Zealand’s environment. It is active as a legal watch-dog, policy think tank, and conference organiser. 3. EDS has an extensive history advocating for positive environmental outcomes for indigenous biodiversity in Aotearoa New Zealand. It has produced several publications that discuss the interface between the Act and protection of indigenous biodiversity. 4. EDS supports reform of the Act. It is important that law designed to stop biosecurity incursions, and manage responses, is modern and up to date. 5. However, EDS considers that the proposed changes need to go further to appropriately recognise and respond to threats to indigenous biodiversity. This submission addresses that overriding imperative under the following topics: the role of the biosecurity system in protecting indigenous biodiversity, provide clearer guidance and prioritisation for indigenous biodiversity from biosecurity threats, long-term management, enable a bespoke funding model for indigenous biodiversity, other proposals that EDS supports, and general biosecurity duty. The role of the biosecurity system in protecting indigenous biodiversity: 6. The biosecurity system plays a critical role in protecting New Zealand’s indigenous species and ecosystems from the threat posed by new biosecurity incursions. 7. Aotearoa New Zealand has the highest proportion of threatened species in the world, with around 4,000 species threatened or at risk of extinction. 8. Thousands of exotic species are now present, many more arrive each year, and some constitute a significant risk to indigenous biodiversity. 9. Climate change is set to exacerbate these risks, creating new pathways for invasive species and increasing the complexity and scale of the management task. 10. At present, while the biosecurity and pest management framework to protect the primary sector is consolidated and coherent, the tools and framework to address biosecurity threats to indigenous biodiversity are underdeveloped. 11. EDS is pleased to see that some changes have been recommended to improve this situation; however, we consider the changes need to go further. 12. The underdeveloped nature of the threat and pest management mechanisms in the conservation system means that the Act is the primary, and in many instances the only, tool for managing an array of invasive species. 13. However, the Act was not designed with the protection of indigenous biodiversity front of mind and its effectiveness at operating in that area is impeded in a number of ways including underdeveloped purpose provisions, failure to recognise the role of the Department of Conservation, and cost-benefit requirements that disadvantage indigenous biodiversity. 14. Reform of the Act is an opportunity to address these problems, and create a more effective and efficient framework that provides robust protection for indigenous biodiversity. Provide clearer guidance and prioritisation for indigenous biodiversity from biosecurity threats: Purpose clause in the Act (Proposals 1 and 2): 15. EDS supports introduction of an overarching purpose clause in the Act. 16. EDS considers that any new purpose clause needs to specifically prioritise the protection of indigenous biodiversity. 17. This express and prominent direction is necessary because impacts on indigenous biodiversity have not been prioritised to date. Ministerial role: strengthen the role of the Minister for Conservation: 18. The Minister for Conservation currently holds no leadership role within the biosecurity system. 19. Although MPI may assign responsibility for pest management decisions to other agencies, in practice this has not occurred very often. 20. It is important that the Minister of Conservation, and by extension DOC, can effectively access the tools and resources available under the Act. 21. Given potential threats posed by species like Caulerpa to indigenous marine biodiversity, we see a compelling case for DOC to play a key role. 22. EDS recommends consideration be given to assigning the Minister of Conservation the role of responsible Minister under the Act in a concurrent capacity. Local knowledge in decision making (Proposal 4): 23. EDS considers that local knowledge, including mātauranga Māori, has the potential to result in better informed biosecurity decisions. 24. We support incorporating local knowledge into decision-making processes for surveillance and prevention. 25. However, caution must be applied to the use of local knowledge as it could include information from vested interests or cause delays. 26. Therefore, EDS considers it critical that scientific knowledge must prevail in the event of a conflict. Interaction with the Freshwater Fisheries Regulation 1983 (Proposals 64 - 67): 27. EDS supports proposal 64 and considers it appropriate that the Act take precedence over sport fish provisions. 28. Regional councils should have greater autonomy to manage pest fish in regional pest management plans. 29. The condition that the fish is causing harm to multiple conflicting values is too broad. 30. The biosecurity system lacks clear statutory levers to prioritise the protection of indigenous freshwater fish. 31. EDS considers that the condition should be amended to properly reflect values adversely affected by pest fish. Surveillance and interaction with the Marine Mammals Protection Act (Proposals 68 and 69): 32. EDS supports proposal 68, emphasising the critical need for robust and timely surveillance activities. 33. However, EDS does not support proposal 69 which would give the Act’s surveillance activities a blanket override of the Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978. 34. Faster decision-making could be achieved by assigning surveillance to DOC or requiring DOC input. Long-term management: Pest and pathway management and small-scale management programmes (Proposals 44 – 49): 35. EDS supports efforts to streamline and speed up biosecurity management planning. Enable more than one entity to share management agency responsibilities (Proposal 49): 36. EDS supports proposal 49 to enable greater coordination between parties, particularly MPI and DOC. 37. Establishing clarity in responsibilities is essential for driving more effective biosecurity responses, as seen with Kauri Dieback disease. 38. Greater collaboration can also be achieved through establishing an emerging risks team. 39. This is particularly relevant for monitoring the spread of Caulerpa and wilding pines. Appropriately factor environmental values into the cost-benefit analysis for pest management plans: 40. The Act requires that the benefits of a plan outweigh its costs, which is problematic for non-economic factors. 41. Under current settings there is a lack of guidance regarding indigenous biodiversity in cost-benefit analyses. 42. Insufficient information about environmental impacts can delay emergency responses. 43. The Act lacks alternative tools to enable decision-makers to accurately quantify environmental effects. 44. The PCE has highlighted that non-market benefits are often overlooked in policy decisions. 45. EDS encourages exploring and implementing non-market valuation methods within the biosecurity framework. 46. Tools also exist to assist decision-makers in assessing the severity of the risk, such as the IUCN Environmental Impact Classification system. Alignment of long-term management outcomes (Proposals 52 - 54): 47. It would be valuable to develop National Policy Direction to guide risk assessment and cost-impact analysis. 48. EDS supports retention and strengthening of section 55 of the Act. Enable a bespoke funding model for indigenous biodiversity: 49. Currently, the Act lacks a specific mechanism to mobilise funding for addressing biosecurity risks to indigenous biodiversity. 50. This gap is evident in the challenges faced by the National Wilding Conifer Control Programme. 51. Industries contributing to the problem should play an active role in funding management. 52. EDS urges the government to establish a sustainable, long-term funding model. 53. This funding model should include contributions from central government, regional councils and industry sectors. Other proposals that EDS supports: 54. EDS supports proposals 7, 8, 39, 41, 42 and 70, which strengthen the biosecurity system. 55. We also support proposal 9 regarding Controlled Area Notices and the Clean Hull Plan. General Biosecurity Duty: 56. We see merit in the introduction of a General Biosecurity Duty (Proposal 40). 57. However, for the duty to be impactful, it must adopt an active approach and be legally enforceable. 58. We support this approach as it has a higher likelihood of effective implementation. Conclusion: 59. EDS supports reform of the Act, but considers that proposed changes need to go further to protect indigenous biodiversity.
